back: Vector: points, lines and polygons with attributes. Raster: a grid of equal cells, each with one value.

front: When is raster better than vector?
back: For continuous surfaces (elevation, rainfall) and images; vector is better for discrete features with sharp boundaries.
A feature identifiable on both a scanned map and a reference, with known real-world coordinates, used in georeferencing.

notes: Aim for less than one cell, preferably half a cell.

back: Nearest neighbour (keeps original values; use for classes), bilinear (smooth), cubic convolution (smooth with sharper edges).
Undershoot (gap), overshoot (extends too far), sliver polygon (thin false polygon between boundaries).

front: How do snapping and topology help?
back: Snapping joins vertices to existing nodes; topology checks find gaps, overlaps and dangles.

front: Effect of halving raster cell size?
back: Four times as many cells for the same area; much larger files.

front: Essential items of a map layout?
back: Title, scale bar, north arrow, legend, source and date.
